keyVerseText: And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ancle bones received strength.
rootMeaning: The Greek noun σφυρόν (sphyrón) is etymologically connected to the concept of a sphere or ball, as it is likely derived from the same root as σφαῖρα (sphaîra), meaning 'sphere.' This connection highlights the rounded, globular nature of the ankle bone, distinguishing it from a simple joint or bone. Understanding this root enriches the English gloss 'ankle' by emphasizing the anatomical shape and function rather than just location.
usageInScripture: This term appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Acts 3:7, where it is translated as 'ankle bones.' The consistency of this translation underscores the word's precise anatomical reference without metaphorical extension in the biblical text. The lexicon also notes metaphorical uses in classical Greek, such as referring to the lower part or edge of a mountain, but such figurative meanings do not appear in Scripture.
theologicalSignificance: The precise identification of σφυρόν as the ankle bone in Scripture reminds us of the incarnational reality of the Christian faith, where God engages with the whole human person, including our physical bodies. The strengthening of the ankle bones symbolizes restoration and the ability to stand firm, reflecting spiritual truths about stability and support found in Christ. This attention to physical detail in Scripture affirms the goodness of the material creation that God redeems. It also encourages believers to trust in God's power to restore not only spiritual health but also physical wholeness.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 3:7 recounts a miraculous healing where Peter lifts a man by the right hand, and 'immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength.' The use of σφυρόν here emphasizes the completeness of the healing, focusing on the very part of the body that enables mobility and stability. This detail enriches the verse by portraying not just a general healing but a restoration of the foundational parts necessary for walking, symbolizing the new strength and purpose given through Christ.
